items.prompt: According to Document 1, how were U.S. senators chosen under the original Constitution of 1787?
options: By the legislature of each state
By the voters of each state
By the House of Representatives
By the president, with the consent of the Senate
why: That is the 1913 rule in the Seventeenth Amendment ("elected by the people thereof"), not the original 1787 rule.
Neither document gives the House any role in choosing senators. The 1787 text says "chosen by the Legislature thereof," meaning each state’s legislature.
You may be thinking of how the president appoints judges with the Senate’s consent. Neither document gives the president a role in choosing senators.
items.hint: Read only the Article I, Section 3 text. Find the word "chosen."
items.explain:
Article I, Section 3 says senators were "chosen by the Legislature thereof," meaning by the legislature of each state.

"By the voters of each state" is the most common wrong answer. That is the rule in the Seventeenth Amendment (1913), "elected by the people thereof," not the original 1787 rule. The House and the president have no role in choosing senators in either document.

items.prompt:
Complete the statement.

Compared with Article I, Section 3, the Seventeenth Amendment changed {{0}} but kept {{1}} the same.

options: who chooses senators
how many senators each state has
how many votes each senator has
the length of a senator’s term
why: Both documents say "two Senators from each State," so the number of senators did not change.
Both documents say "each Senator shall have one vote," so this did not change.
Both documents say "for six years," so the term length did not change.

options: the six-year term for senators
the role of state legislatures in choosing senators
the power of the president to appoint senators
the rule that only property owners could vote for senators
why: The role of state legislatures is exactly what the amendment removed: "chosen by the Legislature" became "elected by the people."
Neither document gives the president any power to appoint senators, so there was nothing to keep.
Neither document mentions property owners. The amendment says voters for senator need the same qualifications as voters for the larger house of the state legislature.

items.hint: Put the two texts side by side and find the only phrase that is different.
items.explain:
Blank 1: who chooses senators. The only substantive change in the first sentence is "chosen by the Legislature thereof" becoming "elected by the people thereof." Both documents say two senators per state, one vote each.

Blank 2: the six-year term for senators. Both documents say "for six years." The role of state legislatures is exactly what the amendment removed. Neither document lets the president appoint senators or mentions property owners.

items.prompt: Prices have been rising quickly across the country. To slow inflation, the Federal Reserve raises interest rates, which makes borrowing more expensive. This action is an example of
options: monetary policy
fiscal policy
a protective tariff
a price ceiling
why: Fiscal policy is taxing and spending by Congress and the president. Here the actor is the Federal Reserve, and the tool is interest rates.
A protective tariff is a tax on imported goods. Nothing in this action involves imports.
A price ceiling is a legal maximum price on a product. The Federal Reserve is changing interest rates, not capping prices.
items.hint: Who is acting, and what tool are they using?
items.explain: The Federal Reserve controls interest rates and the money supply. Changing interest rates to slow or speed up the economy is monetary policy. Fiscal policy is the tempting wrong answer, but it means taxing and spending by Congress and the president.

items.prompt: In Excerpt 2 of Document 2, Jackson argues that government becomes unjust when it
options: passes laws that give special privileges to make the rich richer and the powerful more powerful
fails to make all people equal in talent, education, and wealth through its laws and programs
allows any differences in wealth or social rank to exist among its citizens
taxes farmers, mechanics, and laborers more heavily than it taxes bankers
why: Jackson says the opposite: equality of talents, education, or wealth "can not be produced by human institutions." He does not blame government for failing to create it.
Jackson accepts that "distinctions in society will always exist under every just government." He objects only to artificial privileges added by law.
The excerpt never mentions taxes. This brings in an idea the document does not contain.
items.hint: Find the word "injustice" and read the "when the laws undertake to …" part that comes before it.
items.explain:
Jackson says ordinary people "have a right to complain of the injustice of their Government" when the laws add "artificial distinctions," "exclusive privileges," and favors "to make the rich richer and the potent more powerful." Injustice comes from laws that give special favors to some people.

The idea that government is unjust when it fails to make people equal is the classic misreading. Jackson says equality "can not be produced by human institutions" and that distinctions "will always exist under every just government." The excerpt never mentions taxes.

items.prompt: Read this short passage from a history website. Click the sentence that states an opinion rather than a fact.
spans: It ran 363 miles across New York State, connecting Albany on the Hudson River with Buffalo on Lake Erie.
Before the canal, shipping a ton of goods from western New York to New York City could cost about $100; afterward, the cost fell to $10 or less.
The canal was the greatest public works project in American history.
In the following decades, New York City grew into the nation’s leading port and commercial center.
items.why: The most common wrong click is the shipping-cost sentence, because a big drop in cost sounds like praise. But dollar amounts can be checked in records, so that sentence is a fact claim.
items.hint: Which sentence uses a judgment word that people could argue about?
items.explain: "The canal was the greatest public works project in American history" is a judgment: people could reasonably argue for other projects, such as the transcontinental railroad or the interstate highways. The opening year, the length and route, the shipping costs, and New York City's growth can all be checked in historical records.

items.prompt: In the Senate's vote on overriding the veto on July 13, 1832, a total of 41 senators voted. What is the smallest number of yes votes that would have equaled at least two-thirds of the senators voting?

mistakes.why: That is a simple majority of 41 (more than half). A majority was enough to pass the bill the first time, but overriding a veto takes two-thirds of those voting.
That is the number of yes votes actually cast. The question asks how many would have been needed: two-thirds of 41.
Two-thirds of 41 is about 27.33. You rounded down, but 27 yes votes is only about 65.9% of 41, which is less than two-thirds. Round up to the next whole senator.

items.hint: Total voting = 22 + 19. Find two-thirds of that total. Can a fraction of a senator vote?
items.explain:
Total voting: 22 + 19 = 41 senators.
Two-thirds of 41: 41 × 2 ÷ 3 = 82 ÷ 3 ≈ 27.33.
27 yes votes would fall short (27 ÷ 41 ≈ 65.9%, less than 66.7%).
So at least 28 yes votes were needed. The Senate cast only 22, so the override failed and the veto stood.

A common error is answering 21 (a simple majority) or 22 (the yes votes actually cast).

items.prompt: Use Document 2 and what you know. Drag each event into the correct position to put the events in order from earliest (1st) to latest (5th).

items.why: The most common mistake is placing the veto last. The veto came in 1832, four years before the charter ran out in 1836; Congress was trying to renew the charter early.
items.hint: Use the years in the Background. The Constitution came first, in 1787.
items.explain:
1. 1787: The Constitution is signed. Everything else depends on the powers it created.
  2. 1816: Congress charters the Second Bank for 20 years.
  3. 1819: McCulloch v. Maryland upholds Congress's power to create the bank.
  4. 1832: Jackson vetoes the bill to renew the charter.

options: Homes are spread far apart over hilly land, so each mile of cable or equipment reaches fewer customers.
Rural residents are less interested in using the internet at home than town residents are.
The county does not allow internet companies to build or operate anywhere outside the town.
The graph counts only those households that were surveyed inside the town limits.
why: Nothing in the stimulus describes residents’ interest. This is an assumption, and rural access rose steadily, which suggests demand.
The stimulus never mentions a county ban. This adds a fact that is not there.

The stimulus says the rural area is "hilly and forested" with about 20 people per square mile, compared with about 1,500 in the town. When homes are far apart, a provider must build much more line or equipment for each customer, which makes service slower and costlier to bring. "Rural residents are less interested" is an unsupported assumption, and nothing mentions a county ban.

You divided by the 2025 value (18 ÷ 48). Percent change always divides by the starting value, the 2010 share of 30.
You divided 48 by 30, which gives the new value as a percent of the old one (160%). Subtract 100, or divide the change (18) by 30.

items.explain:
Rural 2010: 30%. Rural 2025: 48%.
Change: 48 − 30 = 18 percentage points.
Percent change: 18 ÷ 30 = 0.6 = 60%.

The most common error is answering 18, which is the change in percentage points, not the percent increase.

items.skill: Separation of powers in a primary source
items.prompt: Which statement best expresses Jackson's view in Excerpt 1 of Document 2?
options: Each branch must judge for itself whether a law is constitutional, not simply follow the Court.
The Supreme Court has the final word on the Constitution, and the other branches must follow it.
Only Congress may decide whether a law is constitutional, because Congress writes the laws.
The president must approve any bill that the Supreme Court has already found constitutional.
why: This describes judicial review, but it is the opposite of Jackson’s argument. He says the Court’s opinion "ought not to control" the other branches.
Jackson names all three branches: "The Congress, the Executive, and the Court must each for itself be guided by its own opinion." He does not give Congress sole authority.
Jackson argues that the Court’s ruling does not bind him. He vetoed the bank bill even though the Court had upheld the bank.
items.hint: Reread: "The Congress, the Executive, and the Court must each for itself be guided by its own opinion of the Constitution."
items.explain:
Jackson says the Court's opinion "ought not to control" the other branches, that "the Congress, the Executive, and the Court must each for itself be guided by its own opinion of the Constitution," and that the president is "independent of both." So he believed he could veto the bank bill as unconstitutional even though the Supreme Court had upheld the bank in McCulloch v. Maryland.

The statement that the Supreme Court has the final word describes judicial review, the principle from Marbury v. Madison (1803), but it is the opposite of Jackson's argument here.

items.prompt: Which option has the lowest cost per household reached?
options: Wireless towers
Satellite vouchers
Fiber-optic cable
Fiber and towers, which tie for the lowest cost per household
why: Vouchers have the lowest total cost, but they reach only 1,000 households: $7,000,000 ÷ 1,000 = $7,000 each, the highest of the three.
Fiber reaches the most households, but $30,000,000 ÷ 5,000 = $6,000 each, twice the cost of the towers.
They do not tie. Fiber costs $6,000 per household and towers cost $3,000. Divide each total by its own number of households.
items.hint: Divide each option’s total cost by the number of households it reaches.
items.explain:
Cost per household = total cost ÷ households reached.

Fiber: $30,000,000 ÷ 5,000 = $6,000
Towers: $9,000,000 ÷ 3,000 = $3,000
Vouchers: $7,000,000 ÷ 1,000 = $7,000

Wireless towers are lowest at $3,000 per household.

Vouchers are the tempting wrong answer because they have the lowest total cost, but they reach so few households that they are the most expensive per household.

items.prompt: Which conclusions are supported by the table? Select two answers.
options: Fiber is the only option that, by itself, would reach more than three-fourths of the 6,000 households.
Towers and vouchers together would reach fewer households than fiber alone.
Vouchers cost the least per household reached.
Towers and vouchers together would cost less than half as much as fiber.
Towers would be finished sooner than either of the other options.
Fiber would reach every rural household that now lacks high-speed internet.
why: Vouchers cost $7,000,000 ÷ 1,000 = $7,000 per household, the most of the three. Their low total cost is the trap.
Towers plus vouchers cost $9 million + $7 million = $16 million. Half of fiber is $15 million, so $16 million is more than half.
Vouchers take 6 months, which is sooner than the towers’ 2 years.
Fiber reaches 5,000 of the 6,000 households, not all of them.
items.hint: Three-fourths of 6,000 is 4,500. Half of $30 million is $15 million.
items.explain:
Supported:

  • Three-fourths of 6,000 = 4,500. Fiber reaches 5,000 (more than 4,500); towers reach 3,000 and vouchers 1,000. Only fiber passes three-fourths.
  • Towers + vouchers = 3,000 + 1,000 = 4,000 households, fewer than fiber's 5,000.

Not supported: vouchers are the most expensive per household; towers + vouchers = $16 million, which is more than half of $30 million ($15 million); vouchers finish soonest; fiber reaches 5,000, not all 6,000.

items.prompt: Which statement best evaluates Dana Whitfield's argument?
options: Her time and cost figures match the table, but her company would bid on the work, so her interest should be weighed.
Her argument should be rejected, because a person who works for an interested company cannot state facts accurately.
Her claim that towers cost about half as much per household as fiber is not supported by the table.
Her argument is based entirely on opinion and includes no specific figures that listeners could check.
why: This goes too far. A personal interest is a reason to check her claims, not proof that they are false, and her figures do match the table.
The table supports her: towers cost $3,000 per household and fiber $6,000, which is exactly half.
She gives checkable figures: two years versus four, and about half the cost per home. Both can be checked against the table.
items.hint: Check each of her numbers against the table. Then reread the sentence that begins "I will be honest."
items.explain:
Whitfield's facts check out: the table shows towers take 2 years and fiber takes 4, and towers cost $3,000 per household compared with $6,000 for fiber, exactly half. But she says her company "would bid on this work," so she has a financial interest. A careful listener accepts the checkable facts while noticing what she left out: wireless is slower, and its equipment must be replaced sooner.

Rejecting her argument just because of her job goes too far; an interest is a reason to check claims, not proof they are false.

items.prompt: Which statement best describes how the two speakers' points of view differ?
options: Whitfield stresses speed and low cost per household; Ortega stresses reach and long-lasting service.
Whitfield believes rural internet access is a serious problem, while Ortega believes it is not urgent.
Ortega opposes spending any county money on rural internet, while Whitfield supports the spending.
Whitfield supports satellite vouchers as a short-term bridge, while Ortega opposes the vouchers.
why: Ortega says many students "cannot get high-speed internet" and wants a solution, so both treat the problem as serious.
Ortega supports spending on fiber and even on vouchers. He does not oppose spending.
This reverses the speakers. It is Ortega who supports satellite vouchers as a short-term bridge; Whitfield never mentions them.
items.hint: First find what they agree on. Then find which criterion each speaker treats as most important.
items.explain:
Both speakers agree that rural families need better internet access. They differ on which criteria matter most. Whitfield emphasizes speed ("running in two years") and cost per household ("about half"). Ortega emphasizes reach ("the most households of any option") and durability ("will last for decades").

The statement about satellite vouchers reverses the speakers: it is Ortega who supports them as a bridge.

items.prompt: A Corland official says, "Our public works program caused unemployment to fall after 2020." Which statement best evaluates this claim using the graph?
options: The claim is weakened, because unemployment fell by about as much in Velstra, which had no such program.
The claim is proven, because Corland’s unemployment fell in every year after the program began.
The claim is weakened, because Corland’s unemployment rose during the years of the program.
The claim cannot be judged at all, because the graph shows unemployment for only one nation.
why: Falling after the program began shows correlation, not cause. Velstra’s rate fell just as much without a program, so something else could explain both drops.
This misreads the graph. Corland’s rate fell from 8.0% in 2020 to 7.0% in 2021 and 6.0% in 2022, during the program.
The graph shows two nations, Corland and Velstra. The second line is exactly the comparison group you need.
items.hint: Compare Corland with Velstra. What would you expect if the program were the real cause?
items.explain:
From 2020 to 2024, Corland's rate fell from 8.0% to 5.0% (3.0 points), and Velstra's fell from 7.8% to 4.9% (2.9 points). Velstra, a similar neighbor, recovered by almost the same amount without a public works program. That comparison suggests the general recovery, not the program, may explain most of Corland's drop, so the claim is weakened.

The tempting wrong answer says the claim is proven because unemployment fell after the program began. A fall that follows a policy is a correlation; the comparison group is what tests the cause.

items.prompt: According to Article I, Section 2 in Document 3, how were enslaved people ("all other Persons") counted when dividing up representatives among the states?
options: Each enslaved person counted as three-fifths of a person.
Each enslaved person counted as one whole person.
Enslaved people were not counted at all.
Only enslaved people who paid taxes were counted.
why: Counting "the whole number of persons" is the 1868 rule in the Fourteenth Amendment, not the 1787 rule.
The 1787 text does not leave them out; it adds "three fifths of all other Persons" to the count. The group left out is "Indians not taxed."
You may be mixing this up with "Indians not taxed." The text says nothing about enslaved people paying taxes.
items.hint: Read only the 1787 text. Find the words "all other Persons."
items.explain:
Article I, Section 2 adds "three fifths of all other Persons" to the number of free persons. "All other Persons" meant enslaved people, so each enslaved person counted as three-fifths of a person when seats in the House were divided up.

"One whole person" is the most common wrong answer. That is the Fourteenth Amendment's rule, "counting the whole number of persons in each State."

items.prompt:
Complete the statement.

Compared with Article I, Section 2, the Fourteenth Amendment changed {{0}} but kept {{1}}.

options: the three-fifths rule for counting people
the exclusion of "Indians not taxed"
the use of population to divide up representatives
the number of senators from each state
why: Both documents say "excluding Indians not taxed," so this did not change.
Both documents divide representatives "according to their respective numbers," meaning population. That stayed the same.
Neither document is about the Senate. Both are about how seats in the House are divided.

options: the exclusion of "Indians not taxed"
the three-fifths rule for counting people
the counting of only free persons
the power of Congress to choose senators
why: The three-fifths rule is exactly what the amendment removed; it now counts "the whole number of persons."
Neither document counts only free persons. The 1787 text also added three-fifths of enslaved people, and the 1868 text counts everyone.
Neither document is about choosing senators. Both are about dividing House seats.

items.hint: Put the two texts side by side. Which phrase disappeared, and which phrase appears in both?
items.explain:
Blank 1: the three-fifths rule. The 1787 text added "three fifths of all other Persons"; the 1868 text counts "the whole number of persons in each State." After slavery was abolished in 1865, the three-fifths rule no longer made sense.

Blank 2: the exclusion of "Indians not taxed." Both texts contain the same phrase. Both also still divide representatives by population.

items.prompt: During a recession, Congress passes and the president signs a law that gives families a temporary tax cut and increases spending on roads and bridges. Which type of economic policy is this?
options: Fiscal policy
Monetary policy
Trade policy
A price control
why: Monetary policy is run by the Federal Reserve through interest rates and the money supply. Here Congress and the president are taxing and spending.
Trade policy deals with imports and exports, such as tariffs. Tax cuts and road spending at home are not trade measures.
A price control sets a legal limit on prices. This law changes taxes and spending, not prices.
items.hint: Who is acting, and what tools are they using?
items.explain: Changing taxes and government spending is fiscal policy, and it is decided by Congress and the president. Monetary policy is the tempting wrong answer, but it is run by the Federal Reserve through interest rates.

items.prompt: In Excerpt 1 of Document 4, Roosevelt proposes to fight unemployment partly by
options: having the government itself hire people to work on needed public projects
cutting taxes on businesses so that private companies will hire more workers
waiting patiently for private businesses to recover and begin hiring on their own
going to war against a foreign nation so that the military will need more soldiers
why: Tax cuts are not mentioned in the excerpt. This brings in an idea from outside the document.
This reverses the excerpt. Roosevelt says the nation is "asking for action, and action now."
Roosevelt compares the task to "the emergency of a war," but that is a comparison. He is not proposing an actual war.
items.hint: Find the words "direct recruiting." What does recruiting mean?
items.explain:
Roosevelt says putting people to work "can be accomplished in part by direct recruiting by the Government itself," while "accomplishing greatly needed projects." In plain English: the government would hire people directly to do useful public work.

The war answer misreads a comparison. "Treating the task as we would treat the emergency of a war" means acting with wartime urgency, not starting a war.

items.prompt: Read this short passage from a history website. Click the sentence that states an opinion rather than a fact.
spans: In 1862, Congress passed the Pacific Railway Act to support a railroad across the continent.
The Central Pacific Railroad built east from Sacramento, California, while the Union Pacific built west from Omaha, Nebraska.
Thousands of Chinese immigrants did much of the Central Pacific’s hardest work in the Sierra Nevada mountains.
The two lines met at Promontory Summit, Utah, on May 10, 1869.
No achievement of the 1800s did more to unite the United States as a single nation.
A trip across the country that had taken months by wagon could now be made in about a week.
items.why: The most common wrong click is the sentence about Chinese immigrants, because "hardest work" sounds like a judgment. But who did the work and where can be checked in company records and historical accounts.
items.hint: Which sentence makes a "most" or "best" kind of claim that people could argue about?
items.explain: "No achievement of the 1800s did more to unite the United States" is a judgment that historians could argue about; someone might name the Union victory in the Civil War instead. The law's date, the routes, the workforce, the meeting place and date, and the travel time can all be checked in records.

items.prompt: In the Ridgeland Senate's vote on overriding the veto on March 27, a total of 38 senators voted. What is the smallest number of yes votes that would have equaled at least two-thirds of the senators voting?

mistakes.why: That is a simple majority of 38 (more than half). A majority passed the bill the first time, but an override takes two-thirds of those voting.
Two-thirds of 38 is about 25.33. You rounded down, but 25 yes votes is only about 65.8% of 38, which is less than two-thirds. Round up to the next whole senator.
That is the yes vote when the Senate first passed the bill. The question asks how many yes votes an override would need: two-thirds of the 38 voting.

items.hint: Total voting = 25 + 13. Find two-thirds of that total, then think about whole senators.
items.explain:
Total voting: 25 + 13 = 38 senators.
Two-thirds of 38: 38 × 2 ÷ 3 = 76 ÷ 3 ≈ 25.33.
25 yes votes falls short (25 ÷ 38 ≈ 65.8%, less than 66.7%).
So at least 26 yes votes were needed. The Senate cast 25, one short, so the override failed.

The most tempting error is 25: rounding 25.33 down. A vote count must reach at least two-thirds, so round up.

items.prompt: Use Document 4 and what you know. Drag each event into the correct position to put the events in order from earliest (1st) to latest (5th).
choices: Congress passes the Social Security Act.
The stock market crashes, and the Great Depression follows.
The United States enters World War I.
The United States enters World War II.
Roosevelt gives his first inaugural address.
items.why: The most common mistake is placing World War I after the stock market crash. The United States entered World War I in 1917, twelve years before the 1929 crash.
items.hint: Use the years in the Background. World War I came first, in 1917.
items.explain:
1. 1917: The United States enters World War I.
  2. 1929: The stock market crashes; the Great Depression follows.
  3. 1933: Roosevelt gives his first inaugural address (March 4).
  4. 1935: Congress passes the Social Security Act.
  5. 1941: The United States enters World War II (December).

items.prompt: Based on the information and the graph, what is the most likely reason the share of Harlan County covered by forest fell from 1990 to 2020?
options: As the population more than doubled, forest was cleared for homes, stores, and roads.
Harlan County residents planted fewer trees each year than residents of other counties did.
A large wildfire destroyed most of the county’s remaining forest in the year 2010.
The graph measures only the forest owned by the county government, not private land.
why: The stimulus never compares Harlan with other counties or mentions tree planting. This claim has no evidence behind it.
No wildfire is mentioned, and the decline is steady (6, 6, then 4 points per decade), not a single sudden drop in 2010.
The title says "share of land covered by forest" for the whole county. Nothing limits it to county-owned land.
items.hint: Reread what the stimulus says about population and new construction.
items.explain:
The stimulus says the population grew from 60,000 to 135,000, more than doubling, and that most growth came as "new subdivisions, shopping centers, and roads" on rolling land near a new highway. Building those requires clearing land, which matches the steady drop in forest cover. This is human-environment interaction: people changing the land to meet their needs.

The wildfire answer is tempting because 2010 is on the graph, but the stimulus never mentions a fire, and the decline is gradual.

items.prompt: By what percent did the share of Harlan County covered by forest decrease from 1990 to 2020?

mistakes.why: That is the change in percentage points (64 − 48). For percent change, divide that change by the starting value: 16 ÷ 64.
You divided by the 2020 value (16 ÷ 48). Percent change always divides by the starting value, the 1990 share of 64.
You divided 48 by 64, which gives the 2020 value as a percent of the 1990 value. The decrease is 100 − 75, or 16 ÷ 64.

items.hint: Find the change, then divide by the 1990 value.
items.explain:
Forest 1990: 64%. Forest 2020: 48%.
Change: 64 − 48 = 16 percentage points.
Percent change: 16 ÷ 64 = 0.25 = 25% decrease.

The most common error is answering 16, which is the change in percentage points, not the percent decrease.

items.skill: Checks and balances in a primary source
items.prompt: Which statement best expresses Madison's main idea in Document 5?
options: Each branch should have the power and motive to resist the others, so ambition checks ambition.
Government is unnecessary, because people can be trusted to control their own behavior.
All power should be concentrated in one branch so that the government can act quickly.
The people alone, through elections, are enough to keep government from abusing power.
why: Madison says government would be unnecessary only "if men were angels." His point is that people are not angels, so government is needed.
This reverses the excerpt. Madison wants to prevent "a gradual concentration of the several powers in the same department."
Madison calls the people the "primary control" on government, but he says experience shows the need for "auxiliary precautions," extra safeguards built into the government itself.
items.hint: Reread the first sentence and the words "Ambition must be made to counteract ambition."
items.explain:
Madison says the best protection against power piling up in one branch is "giving to those who administer each department the necessary constitutional means and personal motives to resist encroachments of the others." In short: "Ambition must be made to counteract ambition." This is the reasoning behind checks and balances.

The idea that government is unnecessary misreads the angels sentence. Madison's point is that because people are not angels, government is needed, and it must be built to control itself.

items.prompt: Which option has the lowest cost per resident brought within 20 minutes of an ambulance?
options: The new ambulance station
The volunteer first-responder training
The two more ambulances at the existing station
The ambulances and the training combined, which cost less per resident than the station
why: The training has the lowest total cost, but $400,000 ÷ 500 = $800 per resident, the highest of the three.
$1,800,000 ÷ 3,000 = $600 per resident, which is more than the station’s $500.
Combined, they cost $2,200,000 for 3,500 residents, about $629 each, which is still more than the station’s $500.
items.hint: Divide each option’s total cost by the number of residents it reaches.
items.explain:
Cost per resident = total cost ÷ residents reached.

Station: $6,000,000 ÷ 12,000 = $500
Ambulances: $1,800,000 ÷ 3,000 = $600
Training: $400,000 ÷ 500 = $800

The new ambulance station is lowest at $500 per resident, even though it has the highest total cost.

The training is the tempting wrong answer because its total is the smallest, but it reaches so few residents that it costs the most per resident.

items.prompt: Which conclusions are supported by the table? Select two answers.
options: The station is the only option that, by itself, would reach more than two-thirds of the 15,000 residents.
The two added ambulances and the training together would cost less than half as much as the station.
The volunteer training costs the least per resident reached.
The two added ambulances and the training together would reach more residents than the station.
The two added ambulances would be ready sooner than either of the other options.
The station would reach every resident who now lives more than 20 minutes from an ambulance.
why: The training costs $400,000 ÷ 500 = $800 per resident, the most of the three. Its low total cost is the trap.
Together they reach 3,000 + 500 = 3,500 residents, far fewer than the station’s 12,000.
The training starts in 4 months, which is sooner than the ambulances’ 1 year.
The station reaches 12,000 of the 15,000 residents, not all of them.
items.hint: Two-thirds of 15,000 is 10,000. Half of $6.0 million is $3.0 million.
items.explain:
Supported:

  • Two-thirds of 15,000 = 10,000. The station reaches 12,000 (more than 10,000); the ambulances reach 3,000 and the training 500. Only the station passes two-thirds.
  • Ambulances + training = $1.8 million + $0.4 million = $2.2 million. Half of the station's $6.0 million is $3.0 million, and $2.2 million is less than that.

Not supported: the training is the most expensive per resident; together the two smaller options reach only 3,500; the training starts soonest; the station reaches 12,000, not all 15,000.

items.prompt: Which statement best evaluates Grant Holloway's argument?
options: His reach and cost figures match the table, but his firm would bid on the station, so his interest should be weighed.
His argument should be dismissed, because a builder who might win the contract cannot give accurate figures.
His claim that the station has the lowest cost per resident is contradicted by the figures in the table.
His argument contains only opinions and offers no specific numbers that listeners could check.
why: This goes too far. His interest is a reason to check his claims, and when checked, his figures are correct.
The table supports him: $6,000,000 ÷ 12,000 = $500 per resident, lower than $600 for the ambulances and $800 for the training.
He gives checkable numbers: twelve thousand residents and about five hundred dollars each. Both match the table.
items.hint: Check his numbers against the table. Then reread the sentence that begins "In fairness."
items.explain:
Holloway's facts check out: the station reaches 12,000 residents, the only option reaching most of the 15,000, and costs $500 per resident, the lowest. But he says his firm "plans to bid on the construction contract," so he has a financial interest. A careful listener accepts the checkable facts while noticing what he plays down: the three-year wait before anyone is helped.

Dismissing him because of his job goes too far; an interest is a reason to check claims, not proof they are false.

items.prompt: Which statement best describes how the two speakers' points of view differ?
options: Holloway stresses reaching the most residents with a lasting plan; Esposito stresses getting help in place quickly.
Esposito believes slow ambulance service is not a serious problem, while Holloway believes it is urgent.
Holloway opposes spending county money on emergency services, while Esposito supports that spending.
Esposito supports the new station as the best long-term plan, while Holloway prefers the volunteer training.
why: Esposito says "people are having heart attacks on these back roads right now," so she clearly sees the problem as serious.
Holloway supports spending $6.0 million on a new station. He does not oppose spending.
This reverses the speakers. Holloway supports the station; Esposito wants the ambulances and the volunteer training.
items.hint: First find what they agree on. Then find which criterion each speaker treats as most important.
items.explain:
Both speakers agree that slow ambulance service is a serious problem. They differ on which criteria matter most. Holloway emphasizes reach ("reaches most of the people at risk"), cost per person, and durability ("lasts for generations"). Esposito emphasizes speed ("on the road in a year," "start this spring").

The answer about Esposito supporting the station reverses the two speakers' positions.

items.prompt: A Dalvian official says, "Raising our interest rate helped bring inflation down." Which evidence from the graph best supports this claim?
options: Dalvia’s inflation fell sharply after 2022, while Ostria’s, with no rate increase, fell only slightly.
Dalvia’s inflation rate was higher in 2022 than it had been in 2021, before the bank acted.
Dalvia’s interest rate stayed at 5.0% from 2023 to 2024, the last two years shown.
Ostria’s inflation rate was slightly higher than Dalvia’s in 2021, the first year shown.
why: Inflation rising from 6.0% to 7.5% shows the problem got worse before the rate increase took effect. It is not evidence that the increase helped.
This describes the policy, not its effect. A steady rate tells you nothing about whether inflation responded.
This compares the nations before Dalvia acted, so it cannot show the effect of Dalvia’s rate increase.
items.hint: Which choice compares a nation that raised rates with a nation that did not?
items.explain:
From 2022 to 2024, Dalvia's inflation fell from 7.5% to 3.0% (4.5 points), while Ostria's fell only from 7.4% to 6.5% (0.9 points). The two nations were similar, and the main difference shown is that Dalvia raised its interest rate. That comparison group is the strongest evidence for the official's claim. Raising interest rates to slow inflation is monetary policy.

The other choices are true facts from the graph, but none of them shows an effect of the rate increase.

stimuli.title: Two Supreme Court Decisions
stimuli.html:
Background: The 14th Amendment (1868) says no state may deny any person "the equal protection of the laws." In 1896, Louisiana law required separate railroad cars for Black and white passengers. By 1954, many states required or allowed separate public schools for Black and white children.

Excerpt A: Plessy v. Ferguson (1896), majority opinion

"The object of the amendment was undoubtedly to enforce the absolute equality of the two races before the law, but, in the nature of things, it could not have been intended to abolish distinctions based upon color…. Laws permitting, and even requiring, their separation, in places where they are liable to be brought into contact, do not necessarily imply the inferiority of either race to the other…."

Excerpt B: Brown v. Board of Education (1954), unanimous opinion

"To separate them from others of similar age and qualifications solely because of their race generates a feeling of inferiority as to their status in the community that may affect their hearts and minds in a way unlikely ever to be undone. … We conclude that in the field of public education the doctrine of ‘separate but equal’ has no place. Separate educational facilities are inherently unequal."

Word help: the amendment = the 14th Amendment; liable to = likely to; them = Black schoolchildren; inherently = by their very nature
stimuli.source: Plessy v. Ferguson, 163 U.S. 537 (1896); Brown v. Board of Education of Topeka, 347 U.S. 483 (1954)

items.prompt:
At a fictional school board hearing on moving the high school start time to 8:45 a.m., a bus company manager says:

"Our company runs 42 buses for the district. Each additional bus costs about $90,000 a year to operate. Later start times are a passing fad. This plan is unfair to working parents, and the board should reject it."

Which statements from the manager are facts that could be checked with records? Select two answers.
options: Our company runs 42 buses for the district.
Each additional bus costs about $90,000 a year to operate.
Later start times are a passing fad.
This plan is unfair to working parents.
The board should reject the plan.
why: "Passing fad" is a judgment about the idea. People can disagree about it, and no record could prove it true or false.
"Unfair" is a judgment word. Whether something is fair is a matter of opinion.
"Should" signals a recommendation, which is an opinion about what the board ought to do.
items.explain: The number of buses and the yearly cost of a bus can be checked in the district's contracts and budget records, so they are facts (fact claims). "Passing fad," "unfair," and "should reject" are judgments, so they are opinions. Also notice the speaker's interest: his company runs the buses, so any change in schedules affects its business. That is a reason to check his facts, not to ignore them.

items.prompt:
Complete the statement using the two excerpts.

The Plessy majority said that laws separating the races {{0}}. The Brown Court said that separating children in schools by race {{1}}.

options: do not necessarily imply that either race is inferior
violate the equal protection promised by the 14th Amendment
are needed to protect the political equality of both races
why: That is the later conclusion in Brown. The Plessy majority upheld separation laws.
The Plessy opinion says the amendment could not have been meant to abolish distinctions; it never says separation protects equality.

options: generates a feeling of inferiority
is acceptable when the facilities are equal
should be decided by each state legislature
why: This is the "separate but equal" idea that Brown rejected. Brown says separate schools are "inherently unequal."
The excerpt from Brown says nothing about leaving the question to legislatures; it decides the question itself.

items.explain:
Blank 1: Plessy says separation laws "do not necessarily imply the inferiority of either race to the other."

Blank 2: Brown says separating children "solely because of their race generates a feeling of inferiority." The two Courts reached opposite conclusions about the same question.

items.prompt: Which statement best describes the relationship between the two decisions?
options: Brown rejected the "separate but equal" reasoning of Plessy for public schools.
Brown applied the reasoning of Plessy to public schools for the first time.
Brown and Plessy both concluded that separation by race does not imply inferiority.
Plessy overturned the earlier ruling in Brown about public transportation.
why: This reverses the relationship. Brown says "separate but equal" has "no place" in public education, so it rejected Plessy’s reasoning rather than applying it.
Only Plessy says that. Brown says separation "generates a feeling of inferiority."
The dates rule this out. Plessy (1896) came 58 years before Brown (1954), so it could not overturn it.
items.explain: Plessy (1896) said separation did not imply inferiority, which supported "separate but equal." Brown (1954) said that in public education "the doctrine of ‘separate but equal’ has no place" and that separate schools are "inherently unequal." So the later decision rejected the earlier one's reasoning for public schools. Always check the dates: a decision can only overturn one that came before it.

items.prompt: By what percent did the urban share of the U.S. population increase from 1900 to 1920? Round to the nearest whole percent.

mistakes.why: That is the change in percentage points (51.2 − 39.6). For percent change, divide that change by the starting value: 11.6 ÷ 39.6.
You divided by the 1920 value (11.6 ÷ 51.2). Percent change always divides by the starting value, the 1900 share of 39.6.
You divided 51.2 by 39.6, which gives the new value as a percent of the old one. Subtract 100 to find the increase.

items.explain:
Change: 51.2 − 39.6 = 11.6 percentage points.
Percent change: 11.6 ÷ 39.6 ≈ 0.293 ≈ 29%.

Answering 11.6 (or 12) gives the percentage-point change, not the percent increase.

items.prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by the graph?
options: By 1920, more than half of U.S. residents lived in urban areas.
The urban share grew by the same number of points in each decade.
Immigration was the main cause of the growth of American cities.
The number of people living in rural areas fell in every decade.
why: The increases were 6.0, 5.6, and 4.9 points. They got smaller each decade, so they were not the same.
The graph shows no data about immigration. A cause needs evidence the graph does not give.
The graph shows shares, not numbers of people. A falling rural share can happen even while the rural population grows, because the total population was growing too.
items.explain: The 1920 value is 51.2%, which is more than half, so that conclusion is supported. The decade-by-decade increases were 6.0, 5.6, and 4.9 points, not equal. The immigration claim brings in a cause the graph does not show. The rural claim confuses a share with a count: the rural share fell, but the graph says nothing about the number of rural residents.

items.prompt: Which statement best describes a trade-off of choosing the street trees?
options: They would serve the most residents, but their full benefit would take years to arrive.
They would cost the least in total, but they would serve the fewest residents of any option.
They would help within a month, but the city would have to pay for them again every summer.
They would cool every neighborhood in the city, but only during the very hottest summers.
why: That describes the fans: the lowest total cost ($60,000) and the fewest residents (800). The trees cost the most.
That describes the cooling centers, which help in a month and must be paid for every summer. Trees take 10 to 15 years to give full shade.
The table says the trees go in "the hottest neighborhoods," serving 20,000 residents, not every neighborhood in the city.
items.explain: The trees serve the most residents (20,000) and last for decades, but full shade takes 10 to 15 years. Gaining reach and durability while giving up speed is the trade-off. The other choices describe the fans or the cooling centers, or claim more than the table says.

items.prompt: A new factory in a fictional country doubles the number of bicycles made each year. The number of people who want to buy bicycles stays the same. What will most likely happen to bicycle prices?
options: They will fall, because the supply of bicycles has increased.
They will rise, because the supply of bicycles has increased.
They will rise, because the demand for bicycles has increased.
They will stay the same, because demand has not changed at all.
why: You have the right cause but the wrong direction. More bicycles for the same number of buyers pushes prices down, not up.
The question says the number of people who want bicycles stays the same, so demand did not increase. Supply changed.
Price depends on both supply and demand. Demand stayed the same, but supply doubled, so the price will change.
items.explain: Supply doubled while demand stayed the same. With more bicycles available than before and no more buyers, sellers must lower prices to sell them. More supply with steady demand means lower prices. The most common mistake is getting the direction backward.

items.prompt: According to the survey, what percent of families gave a pull factor as their main reason for moving?
why: That is the total for the push factors (the mill closing, 42%, plus flooding, 12%). Push factors drive people away from Graybrook.
Jobs in Larkin City are a pull factor, but so are relatives already living there. Add both: 31% + 15%.
The mill closing is the largest single reason, but it is a push factor: it drove families away from Graybrook.
items.explain: Pull factors attract people to a new place: jobs available in Larkin City (31%) and relatives already living there (15%). Total: 31% + 15% = 46%. The mill closing (42%) and flooding (12%) are push factors that drove families away from Graybrook; together they make 54%.

items.prompt:
At a fictional county hearing on limiting lawn watering to two days a week, a farmer says:

"The county's main reservoir is at 38 percent of capacity. My farm uses about 2 million gallons of water each summer. Watering limits are an overreaction by nervous officials. Farmers deserve a bigger share of the water than homeowners do."

Which statements from the farmer are facts that could be checked with records? Select two answers.
options: The county’s main reservoir is at 38 percent of capacity.
My farm uses about 2 million gallons of water each summer.
Watering limits are an overreaction.
The officials proposing the limits are nervous.
Farmers deserve a bigger share of the water than homeowners.
why: "Overreaction" is a judgment about the policy. People can reasonably disagree about whether the limits go too far.
Calling officials "nervous" is the speaker’s characterization of them, not a measurement anyone could check in records.
"Deserve" signals a judgment about fairness, which is an opinion.
items.explain: The reservoir level and the farm's water use can be checked with water utility and farm records, so they are facts (fact claims). "Overreaction," "nervous," and "deserve" express judgments, so they are opinions. The farmer also has an interest: limits on homeowners could leave more water for farms. That is a reason to check his claims, not to ignore them.

items.prompt:
Complete the statement using the two excerpts.

Under the Articles of Confederation, each state kept {{0}}. Under the Constitution, when a state law conflicts with a federal law, {{1}}.

options: every power not expressly given to Congress
no power except what Congress allowed it
only the power to elect members of Congress
why: This reverses Excerpt A. The states kept every power not "expressly delegated" to Congress; Congress did not hand powers down to them.
Excerpt A says each state kept "its sovereignty, freedom, and independence," far more than a single voting power.

options: state judges must follow the federal law
the state law wins inside that state
Congress must vote again on the federal law
why: This reverses Excerpt B. Federal law is "the supreme Law of the Land," "any Thing in the Constitution or Laws of any State to the Contrary notwithstanding."
Excerpt B says nothing about Congress voting again. It settles the conflict by making federal law supreme.

items.explain:
Blank 1: Article II of the Articles says each state "retains its sovereignty… and every power… which is not… expressly delegated" to Congress.

Blank 2: Article VI makes federal law "the supreme Law of the Land," and "the Judges in every State shall be bound thereby," even if state law says otherwise. This is the Supremacy Clause.

items.prompt: Which statement best describes how the Constitution changed the relationship described in the Articles of Confederation?
options: It made national law supreme over conflicting state law, shifting power toward the nation.
It gave each state more power to ignore national laws that its own judges disagreed with.
It abolished the state governments and placed every state under direct national rule.
It kept the balance between the states and the nation exactly as the Articles had set it.
why: This reverses Excerpt B. State judges are "bound" by federal law, even if state law says otherwise.
This goes too far. Article VI settles conflicts between state and federal law; it does not do away with state governments, which still have their own constitutions and laws.
The two excerpts set very different rules: state sovereignty under the Articles, federal supremacy under the Constitution. The balance changed.
items.explain: Under the Articles, each state kept its "sovereignty" and every power not clearly given to Congress. The Constitution's Article VI made federal law "the supreme Law of the Land" and bound state judges to follow it. That shifted power toward the national government while keeping the states (this sharing of power is federalism). The answer about abolishing state governments goes too far: Article VI even mentions "the Constitution or Laws of any State."

items.prompt: By what percent did the foreign-born share of the U.S. population decrease from 1910 to 1970? Round to the nearest whole percent.

mistakes.why: That is the change in percentage points (14.7 − 4.7). For percent change, divide that change by the starting value: 10 ÷ 14.7.
You divided by the 1970 value (10 ÷ 4.7). Percent change always divides by the starting value, the 1910 share of 14.7.
You divided 4.7 by 14.7, which gives the 1970 value as a percent of the 1910 value. The decrease is 100 − 32, or 10 ÷ 14.7.

items.explain:
Change: 14.7 − 4.7 = 10.0 percentage points.
Percent change: 10 ÷ 14.7 ≈ 0.680 ≈ 68% decrease.

Answering 10 gives the percentage-point change, not the percent decrease.

items.prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by the graph and the information above it?
options: The share stayed near 15% from 1870 to 1910, then declined through 1970.
The number of foreign-born people in the country fell in every decade after 1910.
The quota laws of the 1920s were the only reason the foreign-born share fell.
The foreign-born share was higher in 1970 than it had been back in 1870.
why: The graph shows shares, not numbers of people. A share can fall even while the number grows, if the total population grows faster.
The timing fits the quota laws, but "only reason" goes beyond the data. Other events of those years could also have affected immigration.
This misreads the graph: 4.7% in 1970 is far lower than 14.4% in 1870.
items.explain: The share was 14.4%, 14.8%, and 14.7% from 1870 to 1910, close to 15%, and then fell to 11.6%, 6.9%, and 4.7%. The quota laws fit the timing of the decline, but the word "only" makes that claim go too far. The claim about the number of people confuses a share with a count.

items.prompt: Which statement best describes a trade-off of choosing the levee?
options: It would protect the most homes from damage, but it costs the most and takes the longest to build.
It would permanently remove homes from danger, but it requires the families living there to move away.
It is the least expensive option, but it only warns residents instead of keeping water out of homes.
It would protect every home in town from any flood, however large, but only after four years.
why: That describes the buyouts, which remove 40 homes and turn the land into a park.
That describes the warning sirens and sandbags, which cost $300,000 and give warning without stopping water.
The table says the levee protects against floods "up to a set height"; larger floods can go over it.
items.explain: The levee protects 900 homes from damage, more than the buyouts' 40, and the sirens only warn residents. But at $9 million and 4 years, it costs the most and takes the longest. Gaining protection while giving up money and time is the trade-off. The claim that it stops "any flood, however large" ignores the note about larger floods.

items.prompt: A popular video makes a fictional brand of sneakers suddenly fashionable. Many more people want to buy them, but the factory can make only the same number as before. What will most likely happen to the price of the sneakers?
options: It will rise, because the demand for the sneakers has increased.
It will fall, because the demand for the sneakers has increased.
It will rise, because the supply of the sneakers has decreased.
It will stay the same, because supply has not changed at all.
why: You have the right cause but the wrong direction. More buyers competing for the same number of sneakers pushes prices up, not down.
The factory makes "the same number as before," so supply did not decrease. Demand changed.
Price depends on both supply and demand. Supply stayed the same, but demand rose, so the price will change.
items.explain: Demand rose while supply stayed the same. With more buyers competing for the same number of sneakers, sellers can charge more. More demand with steady supply means higher prices. A common mistake is blaming supply when it was demand that changed.

items.prompt: According to the survey, what percent of families gave a push factor as their main reason for moving?
why: That is the total for the pull factors (better schools, 25%, plus job offers, 20%). Pull factors attract people to Fairhaven.
The storm is a push factor, but so is expensive insurance. Add both: 38% + 17%.
You subtracted the storm percentage from 100 (100 − 38). Instead, add every reason that drove families away from Seabright.
items.explain: Push factors drive people away from a place: storm damage in Seabright (38%) and insurance that became too expensive (17%). Total: 38% + 17% = 55%. Better schools (25%) and job offers (20%) are pull factors that attracted families to Fairhaven; together they make 45%.

vocab.def: The simple difference between two percentages.
vocab.example: A turnout rate that rises from 40% to 46% rose by 6 percentage points.

vocab.def: How much a value changed compared with its starting value: (new − old) ÷ old × 100.
vocab.example: A price that goes from $40 to $50 rose by 25%.

vocab.def: The general direction in which data move over time.
vocab.example: Home internet access shows an upward trend from 2010 to 2025.

vocab.def: A relationship in which two things change together; it does not prove that one causes the other.
vocab.example: Ice cream sales and sunburns both rise in summer, but ice cream does not cause sunburns.

vocab.def: A plan of action a government adopts to deal with a public problem.
vocab.example: A county plan to bring internet service to rural homes is a public policy.

vocab.def: A person or group affected by a decision.
vocab.example: Rural families, schools, and internet companies are all stakeholders in a broadband plan.

vocab.def: Giving up one benefit to gain another when you make a choice.
vocab.example: Choosing the faster project may mean accepting slower service.

vocab.def: How much benefit you get for each dollar spent; found by dividing total cost by units of benefit.
vocab.example: A $90,000 program that helps 450 families costs $200 per family.

vocab.def: A document or record created at the time of an event by someone who took part in or witnessed it.
vocab.example: President Franklin Roosevelt’s 1933 inaugural address is a primary source.

vocab.def: A later account that explains or interprets primary sources.
vocab.example: A textbook chapter about World War I is a secondary source.

vocab.def: The position or perspective from which a person sees an issue.
vocab.example: A school principal and a business owner may view the same plan differently.

vocab.def: A one-sided view, often caused by a personal interest, that can affect how information is presented.
vocab.example: A company arguing for a project it would be paid to build may be biased.

vocab.def: A president's rejection of a bill passed by Congress; Congress can override it with a two-thirds vote in each house.
vocab.example: President Andrew Jackson vetoed a bill to renew the national bank's charter in 1832, and the Senate failed to override it.

vocab.def: A formal change or addition to a constitution.
vocab.example: The Seventeenth Amendment (1913) changed how U.S. senators are chosen.

vocab.def: The next-best option you give up when you make a choice.
vocab.example: If a town spends its last $300,000 repaving a road, the opportunity cost is the summer jobs program it could have funded instead.

notes:
Week 10 Study Sheet: Integrated Social Studies Review

Percentage-point change = new rate − old rate  |  Percent change = (new − old) ÷ old × 100
Example: 20% → 30% is +10 points and a 50% increase. Cost-effectiveness = total cost ÷ units of benefit. Two-thirds of a vote: multiply by 2, divide by 3, round up.

Reading Data

  • Title, labels, units, key, source first
  • Describe/compare = safe if the numbers match
  • "Caused" needs a comparison group; "every," "doubled," "only" need checking
  • A share (percent) is not a count

Policy Analysis

  • Problem → Goal → Options → Criteria → Trade-offs → Stakeholders
  • Criteria: total cost, cost per unit, reach, speed, durability, fairness
  • Opportunity cost = next-best option given up
  • Choose what the evidence supports, not what you prefer

Comparing Documents

  • Who? When? Why? For whom? Primary or secondary?
  • Agree, disagree, build on, or change (amend, repeal, overturn)?
  • Find the exact words that differ; check the dates

Evaluating Sources

  • Fact = can be checked; opinion = judgment (best, should, unfair, deserve)
  • Bias = one-sided view, often from personal interest
  • Interest ≠ false: check against neutral evidence
